title: The lowest-cost configuration that meets accuracy goals

opening.headline: When accuracy targets are set but it's unclear how much cost can be reduced, this addresses the method of selecting the cheapest configuration that meets the target.
body: In services with quality targets, errors occur in both directions. Configurations that fall short of the target are unusable, while configurations that exceed the target are usable but incur unnecessary costs. Somewhere between these two errors lies the configuration that meets the target at the lowest cost.

This lesson sequentially examines the reasons for converting accuracy goals into numerical values, the levers for adjusting configurations such as model grade, reasoning strength, prompts, search, and examples, and the principle of selecting the lowest-cost configuration by comparing candidates under the same evaluation criteria.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the trade-off relationship between accuracy goals and cost.
The lowest-cost configuration satisfying the accuracy goal can be determined through candidate comparison.

screens.title: The goal has been set—how far can we reduce it?
screens.lead: Read the following scenario and think about the judgment needed between accuracy objectives and cost.

visual.alt: A conceptual chart showing the underperformance interval below the accuracy target line, the overperformance interval exceeding the target, and the target point in between.

paragraphs: Suppose the accuracy target for the inquiry classification service has been set. The service can only be used if it meets this target. Conversely, configurations that exceed the target can be used, but at the cost of additional expenses proportional to the degree of excess.

Then, where within that range is the most cost-effective configuration? To answer this question, we must create multiple candidate configurations and evaluate them simultaneously using the same criteria for both accuracy and cost. Judging based on just one aspect would be impossible.

OpenAI's accuracy optimization document advises, prior to beginning this discussion, to roughly estimate two values: the cost incurred when the model fails, and the savings or expenses incurred when the model succeeds. A mistake such as refunding a customer $1,000 instead of the correct $100, versus a sentence that sounds unnatural and requires human correction, are not the same error. The scale of the objective emerges from these two values.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Should we set the target accuracy at 90% or 95%? We will summarize how to answer this question at the end of this course.

screens.outro: First, let's check whether the current goal is defined as a number.

screens.title: Think about whether the accuracy target is a number.
screens.lead: When a question is selected, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Before entering or submitting an answer, take a moment to reflect on the goal of my service.

items.prompt: Is my service's accuracy goal defined numerically?
items.answer: If a numerical goal exists, candidate configurations can be compared. If no numerical goal exists, regardless of how many candidates there are, there is no basis to determine which side is better. All comparisons in this class start under the premise that a numerical target exists.

items.prompt: What's the difference between the sentence "It's good" and the sentence "classification accuracy of 90%"?
items.answer: The first sentence is incomparable, while the second sentence can serve as a candidate configuration. Without specifying what constitutes a good fit, it is impossible to determine whether any candidate satisfies the target. Comparison begins with numbers.

items.prompt: What is needed to turn goals into numbers?
items.answer: Measurement data and a benchmark are required. To evaluate candidates accurately, we need a set of predefined answer questions and a standard that indicates whether each response is correct or incorrect. OpenAI's documentation also explains that defining the expected output in advance from a simple prompt is what establishes the meaning of accuracy.

screens.outro: Starting from the premise of numerical targets, we will examine the means for generating candidate configurations.

screens.title: Trade-off between accuracy and cost and configuration candidates
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted in the text, a brief description appears. Check each handle—one for improving accuracy and one for reducing cost.

data.text: Candidate configurations are created by combining various tools. For accuracy-related tools, options include model tier, reasoning strength, prompt optimization, search augmentation, and additional few-shot examples. The OpenAI guide describes prompt engineering, search, and fine-tuning not as sequential steps, but as distinct tools for addressing different types of problems. If the issue involves knowledge the model lacks, Context enhancement is used; if the issue involves format or tone, If inconsistent optimizes the model accordingly. For cost-related tools, options include selecting a smaller model, Token reduction, reducing request volume, and other processing methods such as Batch or Flex. Pricing varies by model and processing method, so each candidate must be individually evaluated for cost.

terms.tip: This approach involves feeding the model with knowledge it has not learned, is outdated, or lacks due to internal company information. This method improves the accuracy of responses.

This is a case where the output format is inconsistent, the tone varies, or the inference procedure is not followed. In such cases, the right direction is to optimize the model's behavior consistency rather than the context.
Methods for reducing the number of input and output tokens. Cost and latency per request both decrease.

This is a processing approach that handles tasks without immediate response requirements asynchronously or reduces costs instead of compromising response speed. The OpenAI documentation recommends using Flex for low-priority tasks such as evaluation or data augmentation.

screens.outro: Now we will present three candidate combinations of the handle for comparison on a single ballot.

screens.title: Present three candidate configurations on the accuracy-cost matrix
screens.lead: The following table shows three candidate results measured from the same evaluation set, assuming identical conditions. Read each row's assessment based on the target accuracy of 90%.

data.caption: Accuracy and relative cost by configuration candidate (estimated values, target accuracy 90%)
rows: Satisfies: The most cost-effective candidate among those satisfying the goal.
Over: Spending additional costs beyond a target of 4 percentage points.
data.notes: The accuracy and relative cost in the table are assumptions made for illustrative purposes. If the evaluation set is small, the accuracy differences among candidates may be due to chance, so candidates near the target line must be re-verified with a sufficiently increased number of evaluation queries. Costs must be calculated separately for each candidate using the unit price and the number of tokens per request. When reading the table, one must avoid the error of selecting C based solely on the accuracy column or selecting A based solely on the cost column. The decision column is the result of aligning both columns against the target line. Furthermore, just because B is at 91% does not mean it has consistently surpassed the target. Since the difference from the target is only 1 percentage point, continuous measurement under operational conditions must be maintained using the same benchmark. When adding new candidates, simply add a new row to the same table and make the decision using the same method. With this single table for comparison, it becomes easy to explain to the team why this configuration was selected, and it also clearly shows which row to move to when the target changes.

screens.outro: I will summarize the principle explaining why selected B is close to the correct answer in the table.

screens.title: Principle of Minimum Cost and Revaluation
screens.lead: Compare the scenario where you alternate between two state buttons and keep a selected configuration unchanged, versus the scenario where you regularly reevaluate the configuration.

states.label: Choose once and maintain
states.body: Even if you initially select the cheapest configuration that meets your goals, over time the assumptions change. A new model might become available, offering a cheaper alternative with the same accuracy, pricing might shift, or traffic and demand patterns might evolve, changing your original goals. If you lock in a configuration, you'll fail to account for these changes, and what was initially the most cost-effective may suddenly become unnecessarily expensive. Conversely, if requirements increase and you keep the same configuration, you may operate below your goals, and it may be difficult to recognize this shortfall.

states.label: Periodic re-evaluation
states.body: When candidates are re-evaluated using the same benchmark set, the changes become immediately apparent. The two principles are: performance exceeding the target is better in terms of cost, and among candidates meeting the target, the one with the lowest cost should be selected. Google Cloud's cost optimization perspective also advises defining and measuring cost and value. To ensure comparability with previous results, the benchmark set must remain unchanged. When updating the benchmark set, previous configurations and new configurations are re-evaluated together using a new benchmark set to establish a consistent basis for comparison. The frequency of re-evaluation should be triggered by events such as the release of a new model, changes in pricing, or significant shifts in traffic.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the principle, let's work through 90% of the cases from start to finish.

screens.title: Case Study on Configuration Changes at a Target Accuracy of 90%
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the decision process for query classification service step by step. Select an arrow to advance one step at a time, following the judgment order.

steps.title: Scenario: 1 million requests per month, target accuracy of 90%
steps.body: We assume a query classification service. There are 1 million monthly requests, with a target accuracy of 90%. The model and configuration are not yet determined, and there is a requirement to minimize costs. All figures are assumed for illustrative purposes.

steps.title: Step 1. Baseline Measurement
steps.body: Apply the base prompt to a small model to evaluate the test set. This result serves as the baseline. If the result is 84%, then there is a 6-point deficit from the target. Without a baseline, we cannot determine how effective any subsequent improvements actually were.

steps.title: Step 2. Cause Identification
steps.body: We gather examples of errors and analyze their root causes. If the issue stems from the model lacking certain knowledge, we enhance context through retrieval; if it's due to formatting or consistency issues, we add a few more illustrative examples. It's essential to select the right approach based on the root cause to ensure cost-effectiveness and efficiency. Simply uploading a large model without understanding the root cause may lead to significant cost increases.

steps.title: Step 3. Candidate Comparison
steps.body: Suppose the enhanced small model achieves 91%, while the large model attains 95% with higher inference strength. Based on a target of 90%, the enhanced small model represents the lowest-cost configuration that meets the target. Although the large model gains an additional 4 percentage points, whether that extra cost is justified depends on the specific target set.

steps.title: Step 4. If the goal changes, reselect the candidates.
steps.body: If service requirements change and the target increases to 95%, a strengthened small model will no longer meet the target. In such cases, we move to candidate C and report the increased cost along with its rationale. Conversely, if delays are permitted, we jointly evaluate whether batch processing can reduce the unit cost while maintaining the same configuration. Thus, for the same service, the lowest-cost configuration varies depending on the target and allowable delay, and the rationale is always based on the accuracy of the evaluation set and the cost per candidate.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: Performance beyond goals is cost.
screens.lead: Let's summarize the key points of this class. Please revisit the questions posed on the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Accuracy targets must be numerical to be comparable. Numbers are derived from evaluation sets and decision thresholds, and the magnitude of the target comes from the cost of failure and the value of success. Tasks where failure is costly—such as refund scenarios—can have high targets, while tasks that can be easily corrected by a person can have lower targets.

After combining components such as model tier, inference strength, prompt, search, and examples, candidates are evaluated together on both accuracy and cost using the same assessment set for comparison. Candidates that fail to meet the target are discarded, while those exceeding the target incur higher costs; thus, the candidate that meets the target at the lowest cost is selected. Among methods to improve accuracy, cheaper options exist beyond larger models, such as context augmentation or adding examples.

Models and pricing requirements change, so the evaluation sets must be regularly re-compared using the same criteria. When returning to the initial question, estimate whether the target is 90% or 95% success based on the approximate cost of failure versus the value of success, and then verify how much impact this choice has on the candidate's cost using a candidate cost table.

callout.text: The accuracy, relative cost, and monthly request volume in the text are assumptions for illustrative purposes. For actual evaluation, calculate using your own assessment set and pricing model.

checks.intro: Based on the comparison table you just viewed, please verify it yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: With a precision target of 90%, and candidates A (small model + basic prompt, 84%, cheapest), B (small model + examples + search, 91%, medium cost), and C (large model + high inference intensity, 95%, most expensive), what would be the optimal choice?
options: B, the cheapest candidate among those satisfying the goal
A, being the cheapest, the goal is set later.
Use both B and C, but respond only with the one that has higher accuracy.
checks.explain: Performance exceeding the target comes at a cost, so we select the cheapest candidate among those meeting the target. A falls short of the target, while C exceeds it.

wrong.1: Configurations that do not meet the requirements cannot be used.
wrong.2: Any part that exceeds the goal only increases costs.
wrong.3: Running both configurations increases costs and provides no justification.

checks.intro: Recall the decision sequence explained a moment ago and arrange it appropriately. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Please review the configuration order for the inquiry classification service (target 90%).
items: Evaluates the dataset with a small model and a base prompt to measure the baseline.
Distinguishes whether the error stems from knowledge deficiency or from issues with form and consistency.
Compares the accuracy and cost of a strengthened small model against a large model candidate.
When the target changes, re-evaluate the candidates and report the additional cost along with the rationale.
checks.explain: The process is: baseline measurement, root cause identification, candidate comparison, and sequential re-evaluation based on goal changes. Only by aligning with the root cause can you select the appropriate solution.

glossary.def: This is a numerical value defined to represent the quality criteria that the service must satisfy, as measurable within the evaluation set.
This is a set of comparison targets combined differently with model tier, reasoning strength, prompt, and search settings.
The principle of selecting the candidate that satisfies the goal and has the lowest cost.
This involves re-comparing candidates using the same evaluation set when price, model, or demand changes.

misconceptions.myth: Accuracy is better the higher it is.
misconceptions.fact: Exceeding goals often only increases costs. The cheapest configuration that meets the goals is optimal.

misconceptions.myth: To improve accuracy, you must only go to larger models.
misconceptions.fact: There may be cheaper alternatives, such as context augmentation or adding examples, that achieve similar effects. To select the appropriate solution, it is first necessary to correctly identify the root cause.

misconceptions.myth: Once established, a configuration remains optimal.
misconceptions.fact: Prices and models change, so the same evaluation set must be regularly re-compared.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The candidate evaluates and compares accuracy and cost together using the same assessment set.
Among the candidate solutions that satisfy the requirements, select the one with the lowest cost.
Model, price, and requirements may change, so it will be reassessed again.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the numerical accuracy goal for my service, and how is that number measured?
